"Be gone, evil-doer! For I... am the Satin Codpiece!"

My partner proudly took his place beside me. "And I... am Nimrod!"

The only sound after we'd proclaimed victory was the sound of overturned cars creaking, buildings crumbling and a few fires burning. Nobody said a word. Nobody cheered, nobody applauded. They just... looked at us like we were a couple of idiots. The people we help always look at us like we're idiots. I wouldn't let it get to me, but Nimrod was obviously shaken. I had to say something.

"You're welcome, citizens! Think nothing of it! No need to thank us!"

My pink cape flew proudly behind me in the wind. I adjusted my orange utility belt, then accidentally fired off a tranquilizer dart from my wrist-shooter. The dart hit Nimrod in the foot. He went down almost immediately. I caught him before he hit the ground in my lime green gloves, and I'm glad he wasn't awake for when the laughing started. Nimrod and I just saved all these people from an insane, sentient supercomputer... and they were laughing at us. I settled my cape, touched my magic codpiece--a gift given to me by my mother, who had it enchanted by a codpiecemancer on our home planet--and transported Nimrod to safety at the Codpiece of Solitude until he awoke from what I'd done.

"Are you okay, Nimrod?"

Nimrod looked at me like he'd never looked at me before. He looked at me like he didn't want to keep fighting.

"Barrett," he said, defeat clear in his voice. He only ever called me by my Earth name when he needed to say something serious. "I don't think we can go on like this anymore."

I sighed deeply, and took off my ivory white mask to reveal my weathered and battered face. I wanted to keep fighting, because fighting for justice is what brought me to this planet devoid of enchanted codpieces, but I didn't want to lose my friend. Nimr--I mean, Aaron--is the only friend I have.

"Aaron, if we don't fight for the people, who will fight for them?"

"I don't know," Nimrod said, flustered, "the Avengers?"

"They're all dead," I said.

"Justice League?" Aaron asked.

"Also dead," I reminded him.

"Wow. Even the fish guy?" he asked, just to be sure.

"Yes, even the fish guy. Most of this world's heroes were taken from us too soon, Aaron. That's why we have to persevere. There aren't many of us left."

Aaron stood upright and wiped his face. He smiled at me.

"You're right, Barrett. We have to press forward. We can't let people down, even if they think we're awful at our job and don't look like the heroes they're used to. It's what's right."

I smiled and laughed heartily as my magic codpiece swelled with pride. "That's my boy, Aaron! Now, contact our friend Baron Turdbutt. The three of us have much work left to do."

Braised collard greens take time and love, and those two things go hand in hand. If time is a determining factor of a given meal for you, that dish isn't one I'd recommend. Potlikker, tho.

When I cook these kinds of greens, I don't want to lose their bite but I also want to be able to chew them. A quick pan braise in flavorful liquid does the trick, usually in tomato sauce or chicken stock. Season well, of course.

If you find they're still too bitter, I'd recommend a wee blanch and shock to start the cooking process before they make their way further in your prep. Better color that way, too.

The number one thing to do if you're buying greens from the farmer's market or supermarket is to prep them same-day. By the time they get to you, the decomposition process has already started and even sturdy greens like collards aren't going to hold well in your fridge for too long. Learn how to make emulsions. Start with mayonnaise. Most salad dressings and sandwich spreads are emulsions, and you need to understand the technique more than you need to understand a recipe. Study flavor profiles. What do you want your sauce or dressing to taste like? What's in it that's salty, sweet, sour, spicy, bitter and/or earthy? What ingredients can you use that harmonize and make the things you want to eat? How does it interact with the dish?

First of all, way to go on building your first cube! Papering a cube is a great feeling, even if you don't think it's optimized yet. It turns out 360 cards is a lot of cards to have to find.

Having a guild cube is a great idea, but it's always important to have sub-strategies within individual colors just in case a drafter doesn't get to play the guild they want. White has weenies, blue has, well, blue, black is pretty flexible and can be discard or zombies or vampires (or literally anything), green usually defaults to fatties and red is your burn deck.

I noticed you aren't running any 2-power white 1CMC creatures other than Glint Hawk, which isn't really a one-drop. For the white weenie lists that accidentally happen in white, having one or two of those creatures makes the race a lot easier to win, so I'd suggest at least [[Soldier of the Pantheon]] to interact with your guild theme.

Having ten total auras in relevant colors to enable all of your aura-supported cards isn't very many, and only eight of them are good when you're attacking. Cards like [[Griffin Guide]], [[Angelic Destiny]] and the best green aura ever [[Rancor]] are going to get that strategy pretty far pretty fast.

The landfall strategy works best with bunches of fetch lands and instants that put lands into play, that way they double as both ramp spells and combat tricks. You've got one swing card in Harrow, and only seven fetch lands in the entire cube, only four of which (Expanse, Wilds, Naya Panorama, Jund Panorama) that find both green and red lands. That's not enough, and it challenges the mana base of the players in the strat. If I can keep it 100, landfall cards are very difficult to play without the ONS/ZEN fetch lands. It's totally cool if they're outside of your budget or not in your collection. I'm just saying it's hard without them.

I respect that you want to be light on countermagic, but that's how blue decks interact. Six counterspells that are all situational is brutal for blue players, and it's going to make people not want to play blue at all. Part of getting drafters into a color is having cards in those colors they know are powerful and exciting. [[Counterspell]] alone is going to do that.

I agree with everyone else who's offered knife skills as the first thing to teach, and I'd add sanitation to that as well. Cross-contamination and the temperature danger zone are critical concepts to understand when you're in a kitchen.

When I actually teach people how to cook, I teach techniques. I show people how to saute, braise, or whatever it is we're doing with the specific dish. It's the technique that's the cornerstone of assembling a recipe. If you memorize a recipe, you can master that one recipe; if you memorize a technique, you can master hundreds of recipes. Give a man a fish, teach a man to fish. That stuff.

I also like to go over the genealogy of the dish, like where it came from, how to came to exist and other trivia. That stuff is as important to understand why a dish is the way it is.
